background:
2 Thessalonians: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

Study notes · dates are approximate and scholars vary

At a glance

2 Thessalonians followed the first letter by a few months, around AD 51. The church was still suffering, and some had been told that “the day of the Lord is just at hand” (2:2), or even already here, so some had stopped working. Paul corrects the confusion and urges them to stand firm.

QuestionTraditional viewNotes
AuthorPaul, with Silvanus and Timothy (1:1)Traditionally Paul; some scholars think a follower wrote it later. Paul signs it himself as proof (3:17).
DateAbout AD 51Soon after 1 Thessalonians, during Paul's stay in Corinth.
Written fromCorinthSilvanus and Timothy were still with Paul (Acts 18:5).
RecipientsThe church in ThessalonicaStill facing persecution and affliction (1:4).
OccasionConfusion about the day of the LordA message, perhaps a letter falsely claiming to be from Paul, said it had already come (2:2).
Practical problemBelievers refusing to workPaul commands, “If any will not work, neither let him eat” (3:10).

The letter has three parts: encouragement in persecution (1), the events before the day of the Lord (2), and instructions about work and discipline (3).

The time map

The shaded band marks about AD 51. Only about ten years earlier, Caligula had tried to set up his statue in the Jerusalem temple.

Emperors who claimed to be gods

Paul's description of one who “sitteth in the temple of God, setting himself forth as God” (2:4) was written in a world that had recently seen such a claim.

  • Caligula (AD 37–41). He demanded worship as a god and in AD 40 ordered a statue of himself placed in the Jerusalem temple. Only delays by the Syrian governor and Caligula's assassination in AD 41 prevented it.
  • Claudius (AD 41–54). Emperor when Paul wrote. He refused some divine honors for himself but was deified after his death.
  • Emperor worship in Thessalonica. The city honored the emperors with a temple, priests and coins; Christians who refused to take part looked disloyal.
  • Forged letters. Letters were often dictated to a scribe. Paul warns of a letter “as from us” (2:2) and signs this one himself to prove it is genuine (3:17).
  • Patrons and clients. Many poorer people depended on wealthy patrons. Some believers may have expected the church to support them instead of working (3:6–12).
  • Justice. Romans prided themselves on justice. Paul assures persecuted believers that God's justice will be perfect when the Lord Jesus is revealed (1:5–10).

Against human powers that claimed divine honor, Paul promises that the Lord Jesus will destroy the lawless one “with the breath of his mouth” (2:8).

A church under pressure

The Thessalonian church was only months old, persecuted, and unsettled by false teaching.

  • Continuing persecution. Paul boasts to other churches about their endurance in “all your persecutions and in the afflictions which ye endure” (1:4).
  • A false alarm. Someone claimed the day of the Lord had already arrived, perhaps through a prophecy, a teaching or a forged letter (2:2).
  • What must come first. Paul reminds them of his teaching in person: a falling away and the revealing of the man of lawlessness, now held back by a restrainer (2:3–7).
  • The idle. Some had stopped working and become busybodies, perhaps thinking the end had come, perhaps relying on others' generosity.
  • Paul's example. Paul had worked night and day to support himself while in Thessalonica, to set an example (3:7–9).
  • Church discipline. Believers were to avoid those who refused to work, yet still warn them “as a brother” (3:14–15).

Around the world in AD 51

2 Thessalonians was written in the middle of Claudius' reign.

RegionWhat was happening
BritainRoman conquest continued after Claudius' invasion of AD 43. The British leader Caratacus was captured in AD 51 and paraded in Rome, where Claudius pardoned him.
RomeClaudius was poisoned in AD 54, most likely by his wife Agrippina, and her 16-year-old son Nero became emperor, guided by the philosopher Seneca.
Armenia and ParthiaFrom AD 58 Rome's general Corbulo fought the Parthians over Armenia, a war that lasted until AD 63.
JudeaUnrest grew under the governors Felix and Festus, with bandits, assassins (the sicarii) and false prophets.
EgyptAlexandria shipped Egypt's grain to Rome every year; its huge Jewish community had survived riots under Caligula.
ChinaThe Eastern Han dynasty under Emperor Ming (AD 57–75). Tradition says Buddhism arrived in his reign.
IndiaRoman ships sailed to southern India with the monsoon winds for pepper; Roman coins have been found there.
The AmericasTeotihuacan near Mexico City was growing into one of the world's great cities.

How the setting shapes the study

Several passages speak directly into the first-century world.

PassageConnection to the times
2 Thess 1:4–7God's just judgment brings rest for the afflicted, in a city where believers had no legal protection.
2 Thess 2:2Letters were dictated and could be forged; Paul warns of one falsely claiming to be from him.
2 Thess 2:3–4Caligula had tried to put his statue in the Jerusalem temple about ten years earlier.
2 Thess 2:6–7The “restrainer” has been understood as the Roman state and its law, God's providence, or the Holy Spirit.
2 Thess 2:15“Traditions” means the teaching Paul passed on in person and by letter.
2 Thess 3:8Paul supported himself by tentmaking rather than take money.
2 Thess 3:10Manual work was looked down on by the elite; Paul honors it.
2 Thess 3:17Paul writes the greeting in his own hand, as ancient letter writers did to show authenticity.

Paul's answer to fear and confusion is steady faithfulness: “be not weary in well-doing” (3:13).

Maps: then and now

Paul traveled west along the Via Egnatia from Philippi to Thessalonica, about 90 miles, then fled to Berea and went on by sea or road to Athens and Corinth.

Today Thessalonica is Thessaloniki, Greece's second-largest city. Its Roman forum and the later Arch of Galerius can be seen downtown.

items.text: Thanksgiving and God's Just Judgment
Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy, unto the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ;
Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
We are bound to give thanks to God always for you, brethren, even as it is meet, for that your faith groweth exceedingly, and the love of each one of you all toward one another aboundeth;
so that we ourselves glory in you in the churches of God for your patience and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions which ye endure;
which is a manifest token of the righteous judgment of God; to the end that ye may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which ye also suffer:
if so be that it is a righteous thing with God to recompense affliction to them that afflict you,
and to you that are afflicted rest with us, at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power in flaming fire,
rendering vengeance to them that know not God, and to them that obey not the gospel of our Lord Jesus:
who shall suffer punishment, even eternal destruction from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might,
when he shall come to be glorified in his saints, and to be marvelled at in all them that believed (because our testimony unto you was believed) in that day.
To which end we also pray always for you, that our God may count you worthy of your calling, and fulfil every desire of goodness and every work of faith, with power;
that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and ye in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.

summary.title: CHAPTER 1 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul thanks God because the Thessalonians' faith is growing abundantly and their love for one another is increasing, and he boasts about their endurance in persecution. Their suffering is evidence of God's righteous judgment: they are being counted worthy of His kingdom. God will repay with affliction those who afflict them and grant rest to the afflicted when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with His mighty angels in flaming fire. Those who do not know God or obey the gospel will suffer eternal destruction away from His presence, when He comes to be glorified in His saints. Paul prays that God will make them worthy of their calling and fulfill every good purpose, so that the name of Jesus is glorified in them and they in Him.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What does Paul say about God's justice in verses 5–10, and what does he pray will happen in the believers in verses 11–12?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: How would persecuted believers in Thessalonica, likely facing pressure from neighbors and local authorities, have received the promise of rest and righteous judgment (vv. 6–7)?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul boasts about the Thessalonians' growing faith amid suffering (vv. 3–4); how can you notice and name endurance in someone who is struggling?

items.text: The Man of Lawlessness
Now we beseech you, brethren, touching the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and our gathering together unto him;
to the end that ye be not quickly shaken from your mind, nor yet be troubled, either by spirit, or by word, or by epistle as from us, as that the day of the Lord is just at hand;
let no man beguile you in any wise: for it will not be, except the falling away come first, and the man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition,
he that opposeth and exalteth himself against all that is called God or that is worshipped; so that he sitteth in the temple of God, setting himself forth as God.
Remember ye not, that, when I was yet with you, I told you these things?
And now ye know that which restraineth, to the end that he may be revealed in his own season.
For the mystery of lawlessness doth already work: only there is one that restraineth now, until he be taken out of the way.
And then shall be revealed the lawless one, whom the Lord Jesus shall slay with the breath of his mouth, and bring to nought by the manifestation of his coming;
even he, whose coming is according to the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders,
and with all deceit of unrighteousness for them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved.
And for this cause God sendeth them a working of error, that they should believe a lie:
that they all might be judged who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.
Stand Firm
But we are bound to give thanks to God always for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, for that God chose you from the beginning unto salvation in sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth:
whereunto he called you through our gospel, to the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
So then, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye were taught, whether by word, or by epistle of ours.
Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace,
comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word.

summary.title: CHAPTER 2 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul asks them not to be quickly shaken or alarmed by any spirit, word or letter claiming that the day of the Lord has already come. That day will not come unless the falling away comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, who exalts himself against every so-called god and sits in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God. Something now restrains him until the right time.

The mystery of lawlessness is already at work, but when the lawless one is revealed, the Lord Jesus will slay him with the breath of His mouth and destroy him by the appearance of His coming. His coming will be with false signs and wonders that deceive those who refused to love the truth. But Paul gives thanks for the Thessalonians, whom God chose for salvation through sanctification and belief in the truth. He urges them to stand firm and hold the traditions they were taught, and prays for God to comfort and establish them.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What false report troubled the church according to verses 1–2, and what does Paul say must come first (vv. 3–4)?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why might a forged letter or rumor claiming the day of the Lord had come (v. 2) have unsettled a young church already under pressure?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul tells them to stand fast and hold the traditions they were taught (v. 15); what helps you stay steady when alarming claims circulate?

items.text: Pray for Us
Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, even as also it is with you;
and that we may be delivered from unreasonable and evil men; for all have not faith.
But the Lord is faithful, who shall establish you, and guard you from the evil one.
And we have confidence in the Lord touching you, that ye both do and will do the things which we command.
And the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God, and into the patience of Christ.
Warning Against Idleness
Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which they received of us.
For yourselves know how ye ought to imitate us: for we behaved not ourselves disorderly among you;
neither did we eat bread for nought at any man’s hand, but in labor and travail, working night and day, that we might not burden any of you:
not because we have not the right, but to make ourselves an ensample unto you, that ye should imitate us.
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, If any will not work, neither let him eat.
For we hear of some that walk among you disorderly, that work not at all, but are busybodies.
Now them that are such we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ, that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread.
But ye, brethren, be not weary in well-doing.
And if any man obeyeth not our word by this epistle, note that man, that ye have no company with him, to the end that he may be ashamed.
And yet count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.
Final Blessing and Paul's Signature
Now the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in all ways. The Lord be with you all.
The salutation of me Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle: so I write.
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.

summary.title: CHAPTER 3 IN SUMMARY
paras: Paul asks for prayer that the word of the Lord may spread rapidly and be glorified, and that he may be delivered from wicked men, for not all have faith. “But the Lord is faithful, who shall establish you, and guard you from the evil one.” He is confident they will keep doing what he commands, and prays that the Lord will direct their hearts into God's love and Christ's patience.

He commands them to keep away from any brother who walks in idleness. Paul set an example by working night and day so as not to be a burden, and he laid down the rule, “If any will not work, neither let him eat.” The idle must work quietly and earn their own living, and the rest must not grow weary in doing good. Anyone who refuses should be noted and avoided, yet admonished as a brother. Paul signs the greeting in his own hand and prays for peace and grace for them all.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What instructions does Paul give about those who walk disorderly in verses 6–15, and how should the church treat them?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why would Paul's own example of working night and day (vv. 7–9) carry weight in a city where some believers had stopped working?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul says to count the disobedient not as an enemy but to admonish him as a brother (v. 15); how could you correct someone without cutting them off?

wrap.title: 2 Thessalonians In Summary
paras: 2 Thessalonians is a short follow-up to Paul's first letter. The young church was still suffering persecution, and new confusion had arisen: someone claimed that the day of the Lord had already come. Some believers were alarmed, and some had stopped working altogether.

Paul begins with encouragement. The church's growing faith and love under persecution show that God is counting them worthy of His kingdom. God is just, and He will set things right when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven: the afflicted will find rest, and those who reject God and the gospel will face judgment.

In chapter 2 Paul corrects the false teaching. Before the day of the Lord, a rebellion must come and the man of lawlessness must be revealed, one who sets himself up as God in God's temple. His power is real but limited, for something restrains him now, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him at His coming. Written not long after Caligula tried to put his statue in the Jerusalem temple, these words had a vivid background.

In chapter 3 Paul turns to everyday faithfulness. Believers must keep working, as Paul did, and not live off others; “If any will not work, neither let him eat.” The church should lovingly discipline those who refuse, and everyone should keep on doing good.

The message in one line: the Lord Jesus will certainly return to bring justice and rest, so believers should not be shaken by fear or rumors, but stand firm in the truth and keep faithfully doing good while they wait.
